item.title: Context parallelism
item.description:
Context Parallelism (CP)—often referred to as Sequence Parallelism across nodes, or realized via primitives like RingAttention and DeepSpeed-Ulysses—is an intra-layer distributed training and inference paradigm that partitions the sequence (context) dimension SSS across PPP accelerators while leaving the model’s weight matrices intact on each rank.

Where Tensor Parallelism (TP) splits the hidden dimension hhh (or attention heads hheadsh_{\text{heads}}hheads​) and hits an intra-node barrier (P≤8P \le 8P≤8), Context Parallelism enables scaling sequence lengths to hundreds of thousands or millions of tokens (S≥1MS \ge 1\text{M}S≥1M) across multi-node clusters by distributing activation memory and compute quadratically tied to sequence length.

1. The Scaling Bottleneck CP Resolves

In standard Transformer architectures, self-attention memory and compute scale with sequence length SSS:

  • Compute (FLOPs): O(S2⋅d)\mathcal{O}(S^2 \cdot d)O(S2⋅d) per head.
  • Activation Memory: Attention logits require O(B⋅h⋅S2)\mathcal{O}(B \cdot h \cdot S^2)O(B⋅h⋅S2) in vanilla attention, or O(B⋅h⋅S⋅d)\mathcal{O}(B \cdot h \cdot S \cdot d)O(B⋅h⋅S⋅d) under online Softmax engines like FlashAttention.
  • KV Cache (Inference): Scales linearly with SSS per request: 2×2×B×S×L×hKV×dk2 \times 2 \times B \times S \times L \times h_{KV} \times d_k2×2×B×S×L×hKV​×dk​ bytes.

When scaling S→128kS \to 128\text{k}S→128k or 1M1\text{M}1M, a single GPU’s High-Bandwidth Memory (HBM) is overwhelmed by activations even if the model weights fit completely. TP cannot shard SSS inside the core attention computation without cross-head communication, and Pipeline Parallelism (PP) requires activations of the entire sequence to be buffered between stage handoffs. Context Parallelism directly addresses this by slicing inputs:

X∈RB×S×d  ⟹  X(p)∈RB×SP×d,p∈{0,1,…,P−1} X \in \mathbb{R}^{B \times S \times d} \implies X^{(p)} \in \mathbb{R}^{B \times \frac{S}{P} \times d}, \quad p \in \{0, 1, \dots, P-1\} X∈RB×S×d⟹X(p)∈RB×PS​×d,p∈{0,1,…,P−1}

Each rank holds a sub-sequence of length s=S/Ps = S/Ps=S/P.

2. The Core Challenge: Cross-Rank Attention

Feedforward networks (MLPs), RMSNorm/LayerNorm, and embedding lookups operate element-wise or across token features independently. Sharding along SSS means these layers run locally on rank ppp with zero cross-rank communication:

HMLP(p)=MLP(X(p)) H_{\text{MLP}}^{(p)} = \text{MLP}\left(X^{(p)}\right) HMLP(p)​=MLP(X(p))

The fundamental challenge arises strictly at Self-Attention: token iii on rank ppp must attend to all tokens j≤ij \le ij≤i (under causal masking) or all tokens j∈[0,S−1]j \in [0, S-1]j∈[0,S−1] (under bidirectional attention), many of which reside in the memory of ranks q≠pq \ne pq=p.

Two primary architectures have emerged to solve this: RingAttention and DeepSpeed-Ulysses.

3. Paradigm A: RingAttention (P2P Overlapped Rings)

Proposed by Hao Liu et al., RingAttention distributes the query, key, and value sequences across a logical ring of PPP GPUs.

Sharding

Each GPU ppp permanently holds its local chunk of Queries, Keys, and Values:

Q(p),K(p),V(p)∈RB×SP×h×dk Q^{(p)}, K^{(p)}, V^{(p)} \in \mathbb{R}^{B \times \frac{S}{P} \times h \times d_k} Q(p),K(p),V(p)∈RB×PS​×h×dk​

Execution Loop

Instead of collecting all Keys and Values globally via an All-Gather (which would trigger an out-of-memory exception), RingAttention streams KKK and VVV in a bucket-brigade ring across PPP steps:

Step 0: GPU p computes Attention(Q^(p), K^(p), V^(p))
│
├── P2P Send K^(p), V^(p) to GPU (p + 1)
└── P2P Recv K^(p-1), V^(p-1) from GPU (p - 1)
│
Step 1: GPU p computes Attention(Q^(p), K^(p-1), V^(p-1)) [Overlapped with step 2 transfer]
│
└── ... repeat for P - 1 shifts ...
┌───────────────────────────────┐
▼ │
[GPU 0] ──► (K, V) ──► [GPU 1] ──► [GPU 2] ──► [GPU 3] ──┐
▲ │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Online Softmax Rescaling

Because Q(p)Q^{(p)}Q(p) attends to blocks of (K,V)(K, V)(K,V) arriving asynchronously over PPP ring steps, the standard Softmax normalization factor ∑eq⋅k\sum e^{q \cdot k}∑eq⋅k cannot be computed upfront. RingAttention integrates Online Softmax (the core mathematical engine of FlashAttention):

For each block step k∈[0,P−1]k \in [0, P-1]k∈[0,P−1], rank ppp maintains running statistics:

  • Local maximum logit: mi(k)∈Rm_i^{(k)} \in \mathbb{R}mi(k)​∈R
  • Running denominator sum: ℓi(k)∈R\ell_i^{(k)} \in \mathbb{R}ℓi(k)​∈R
  • Partial output accumulator: Oi(k)∈RdkO_i^{(k)} \in \mathbb{R}^{d_k}Oi(k)​∈Rdk​

When a new incoming block Knew,VnewK_{\text{new}}, V_{\text{new}}Knew​,Vnew​ is processed:

  1. Compute local raw scores: Snew=Q(p)KnewT/dkS_{\text{new}} = Q^{(p)} K_{\text{new}}^T / \sqrt{d_k}Snew​=Q(p)KnewT​/dk​​
  2. Update local max: minext=max⁡(mi(k), max⁡(Snew))m_i^{\text{next}} = \max(m_i^{(k)}, \, \max(S_{\text{new}}))minext​=max(mi(k)​,max(Snew​))
  3. Rescale running sum and output accumulator: ℓinext=ℓi(k)⋅emi(k)−minext+∑eSnew−minext \ell_i^{\text{next}} = \ell_i^{(k)} \cdot e^{m_i^{(k)} - m_i^{\text{next}}} + \sum e^{S_{\text{new}} - m_i^{\text{next}}} ℓinext​=ℓi(k)​⋅emi(k)​−minext​+∑eSnew​−minext​ Oinext=Oi(k)⋅(ℓi(k)emi(k)−minextℓinext)+Softmax(Snew−minext)Vnew⋅(eminextℓinext) O_i^{\text{next}} = O_i^{(k)} \cdot \left(\frac{\ell_i^{(k)} e^{m_i^{(k)} - m_i^{\text{next}}}}{\ell_i^{\text{next}}}\right) + \text{Softmax}\left(S_{\text{new}} - m_i^{\text{next}}\right) V_{\text{new}} \cdot \left(\frac{e^{m_i^{\text{next}}}}{\ell_i^{\text{next}}}\right) Oinext​=Oi(k)​⋅(ℓinext​ℓi(k)​emi(k)​−minext​​)+Softmax(Snew​−minext​)Vnew​⋅(ℓinext​eminext​​)

At step P−1P-1P−1, OiO_iOi​ holds the exact mathematical result without any single GPU ever holding the complete sequence.

Compute-Communication Overlap

RingAttention completely hides network latency if the time to compute local attention on a block of size SP\frac{S}{P}PS​ exceeds the point-to-point (P2P) transfer time of (K,V)(K, V)(K,V) over interconnect links:

Tcompute=4⋅B⋅(S/P)2⋅h⋅dkFLOPsGPU≥Tcomm=2⋅B⋅(S/P)⋅hKV⋅dk×sizeof(FP16)Bandwidthlink T_{\text{compute}} = \frac{4 \cdot B \cdot (S/P)^2 \cdot h \cdot d_k}{\text{FLOPs}_{\text{GPU}}} \quad \ge \quad T_{\text{comm}} = \frac{2 \cdot B \cdot (S/P) \cdot h_{KV} \cdot d_k \times \text{sizeof(FP16)}}{\text{Bandwidth}_{\text{link}}} Tcompute​=FLOPsGPU​4⋅B⋅(S/P)2⋅h⋅dk​​≥Tcomm​=Bandwidthlink​2⋅B⋅(S/P)⋅hKV​⋅dk​×sizeof(FP16)​

As long as the per-GPU token chunk SP\frac{S}{P}PS​ is large enough (typically ≥2k−4k\ge 2\text{k} - 4\text{k}≥2k−4k tokens), communication is 100% hidden behind compute.

4. Causal Masking Imbalance and Striped RingAttention

In causal auto-regressive models, token iii can only attend to token jjj where j≤ij \le ij≤i.

If sequences are sliced contiguously into linear chunks:

  • GPU 0 gets tokens [0,SP−1][0, \frac{S}{P}-1][0,PS​−1]: It only computes self-attention on its own tokens; all subsequent ring chunks from GPUs 1…P−11 \dots P-11…P−1 are masked out (0%0\%0% compute on those steps).
  • GPU P−1P-1P−1 gets tokens [(P−1)SP,S−1][\frac{(P-1)S}{P}, S-1][P(P−1)S​,S−1]: It must attend to all past tokens (100%100\%100% compute across all PPP steps).

This creates an extreme compute imbalance where GPU 0 sits idle while GPU P−1P-1P−1 bottlenecks the cluster, yielding ~50% hardware underutilization.

Naive Block Assignment:
GPU 0: [■ □ □ □] -> 25% compute
GPU 1: [■ ■ □ □] -> 50% compute
GPU 2: [■ ■ ■ □] -> 75% compute
GPU 3: [■ ■ ■ ■] -> 100% compute (Bottleneck)

Striped Partitioning (Round-Robin Slicing)

To restore perfect load balance, Striped Attention maps tokens to GPUs using an interleaved round-robin stride:

Token t  ⟹  GPU (t mod P) \text{Token } t \implies \text{GPU } (t \bmod P) Token t⟹GPU (tmodP)

Each GPU holds an evenly distributed mixture of early, middle, and late tokens. The number of active causal attention pairs is virtually identical across all PPP ranks throughout the ring rotations, returning hardware compute efficiency to near 100%100\%100%.

5. Paradigm B: DeepSpeed-Ulysses (All-to-All Transposition)

While RingAttention uses circular asynchronous P2P, DeepSpeed-Ulysses leverages global All-to-All collective communication primitives to swap between sequence partitioning and attention-head partitioning.

Input: Slices along Sequence [S/P, H]
│
▼
[ All-to-All-v Collective ] <-- Transposes (S/P, H) -> (S, H/P)
│
▼
Compute Attention locally on [S, H/P] via FlashAttention (Full Sequence, Subset of Heads)
│
▼
[ All-to-All-v Collective ] <-- Transposes (S, H/P) -> (S/P, H)
│
▼
Output: Slices along Sequence [S/P, H]
  1. Before Attention: Activations are partitioned along sequence length SP\frac{S}{P}PS​, holding all heads HHH.
  2. First All-to-All: Ranks exchange slices so each GPU now holds the entire sequence length SSS, but only a subset of heads HP\frac{H}{P}PH​.
  3. Local Compute: Standard optimized FlashAttention runs locally on full context SSS for HP\frac{H}{P}PH​ heads with zero custom communication or online softmax stitching.
  4. Second All-to-All: The attention output tensor is transposed back from [S,HP][S, \frac{H}{P}][S,PH​] to [SP,H][\frac{S}{P}, H][PS​,H] to resume element-wise MLP computation.

DeepSpeed-Ulysses vs. RingAttention Trade-offs

Dimension RingAttention DeepSpeed-Ulysses
Communication Type Asynchronous Non-blocking P2P (ISend / IRecv) Synchronous Collective (All-to-All)
Head Constraint Works with any head configuration (even MQA where hKV=1h_{KV}=1hKV​=1) Requires total attention heads divisible by PPP (H mod P=0H \bmod P = 0HmodP=0)
Interconnect Sensitivity Tolerant of lower bandwidths (e.g., inter-node RoCE/Infiniband) via overlap Demands ultra-high bisection bandwidth (NVSwitch / high-tier InfiniBand)
Implementation Complexity High (custom Online Softmax loop + CUDA/Triton ring management) Low (wraps native FlashAttention inside two All-to-All collectives)
Memory Ceiling Independent of PPP; scales arbitrarily to millions of tokens Max sequence SSS constrained by whether a single GPU can hold [S,HP][S,\tfrac{H}{P}][S,PH​] in memory

6. Integration in 4D Parallelism (TP + PP + DP/FSDP + CP)

In large-scale production training (e.g., Llama 3, DeepSeek-V3), Context Parallelism forms a dedicated dimension in the parallel process grid:

World Size=TP×PP×DP (FSDP)×CP \text{World Size} = \text{TP} \times \text{PP} \times \text{DP (FSDP)} \times \text{CP} World Size=TP×PP×DP (FSDP)×CP
  • Intra-node: Tensor Parallelism (TP ≤8\le 8≤8) operates within a single NVLink domain due to sub-microsecond latency demands.
  • Low-tier Inter-node: Context Parallelism (CP) operates across nearby nodes, hiding inter-node network latency behind the compute of large sequence chunks.
  • Global Grid: ZeRO-3 / FSDP shards optimizer states across the data-parallel group, while Pipeline Parallelism (PP) connects distant clusters or stages across minimal communication boundaries.

During backpropagation, CP requires reversing the communication ring or re-executing All-to-All to distribute activation gradients ∇Q,∇K,∇V\nabla_Q, \nabla_K, \nabla_V∇Q​,∇K​,∇V​, maintaining an identical memory footprint reduction throughout the backward pass.

item.title: TP + SP
item.description:
Tensor Parallelism (TP) is an intra-layer model-parallelism technique that splits individual weight matrices, matrix multiplications (GEMMs), and activations across multiple accelerators (GPUs/TPUs).

Unlike Pipeline Parallelism (PP)—which partitions models across sequential layers and introduces execution bubbles—or Data Parallelism (DP/FSDP)—which replicates model weights or shards parameters across batch dimensions—Tensor Parallelism splits individual weight tensors within a layer to compute a single layer cooperatively across multiple ranks.

1. Mathematical Foundations: 1D Matrix Partitioning

Consider a standard fully connected layer computing Y=Activation(XW)Y = \text{Activation}(XW)Y=Activation(XW), where:

  • Input activation X∈RB×dinX \in \mathbb{R}^{B \times d_{in}}X∈RB×din​ (batch size B×B \timesB× sequence length SSS, flattened to dimension BBB)
  • Weight matrix W∈Rdin×doutW \in \mathbb{R}^{d_{in} \times d_{out}}W∈Rdin​×dout​
  • Output activation Y∈RB×doutY \in \mathbb{R}^{B \times d_{out}}Y∈RB×dout​

Across NNN parallel processing ranks, a matrix multiplication can be sliced along its columns or its rows.

Column-Parallel Linear Layer

The weight matrix WWW is sliced along its column dimension into NNN equal chunks:

W=[W1W2…WN],Wi∈Rdin×doutN W = \begin{bmatrix} W_1 & W_2 & \dots & W_N \end{bmatrix}, \quad W_i \in \mathbb{R}^{d_{in} \times \frac{d_{out}}{N}} W=[W1​​W2​​…​WN​​],Wi​∈Rdin​×Ndout​​

Each GPU iii holds the full input XXX and its local shard WiW_iWi​:

Yi=XWi∈RB×doutN Y_i = X W_i \in \mathbb{R}^{B \times \frac{d_{out}}{N}} Yi​=XWi​∈RB×Ndout​​

Because linear matrix multiplication is distributive across columns:

Y=[Y1Y2…YN] Y = \begin{bmatrix} Y_1 & Y_2 & \dots & Y_N \end{bmatrix} Y=[Y1​​Y2​​…​YN​​]

If an element-wise non-linearity σ\sigmaσ (e.g., GeLU, SwiGLU) is applied, it commutes with column concatenation:

σ(Y)=[σ(Y1)σ(Y2)…σ(YN)] \sigma(Y) = \begin{bmatrix} \sigma(Y_1) & \sigma(Y_2) & \dots & \sigma(Y_N) \end{bmatrix} σ(Y)=[σ(Y1​)​σ(Y2​)​…​σ(YN​)​]
  • Forward pass: Each rank computes YiY_iYi​ locally with zero communication.
  • Communication required: None yet, as long as the subsequent operation can consume column-sharded tensors.

Row-Parallel Linear Layer

The weight matrix WWW is sliced along its row (contracting) dimension:

W=[W1W2⋮WN],Wi∈RdinN×dout W = \begin{bmatrix} W_1 \\ W_2 \\ \vdots \\ W_N \end{bmatrix}, \quad W_i \in \mathbb{R}^{\frac{d_{in}}{N} \times d_{out}} W=​W1​W2​⋮WN​​​,Wi​∈RNdin​​×dout​

To match dimensions, the input XXX must be partitioned along its column dimension: X=[X1,X2,…,XN]X = [X_1, X_2, \dots, X_N]X=[X1​,X2​,…,XN​], where Xi∈RB×dinNX_i \in \mathbb{R}^{B \times \frac{d_{in}}{N}}Xi​∈RB×Ndin​​.

Each rank computes a local partial product:

Zi=XiWi∈RB×dout Z_i = X_i W_i \in \mathbb{R}^{B \times d_{out}} Zi​=Xi​Wi​∈RB×dout​

The full mathematical output YYY is the summation of these partial products:

Y=∑i=1NZi=∑i=1NXiWi=XW Y = \sum_{i=1}^N Z_i = \sum_{i=1}^N X_i W_i = XW Y=i=1∑N​Zi​=i=1∑N​Xi​Wi​=XW
  • Forward pass: Requires an All-Reduce (sum) collective across all NNN ranks to aggregate ZiZ_iZi​ into YYY.

2. The Megatron-LM Coupling Principle

Naively chaining parallel layers requires an All-Gather after each column-parallel layer and an All-Reduce after each row-parallel layer, creating substantial collective communication overhead.

The core insight of Megatron-LM is pairing Column-Parallel and Row-Parallel layers back-to-back to cancel intermediate communications.

MLP Forward Pass:
X (Replicated)
│
├──► GPU 0: [W1_col] ──► GeLU ──► [W2_row] ──┐
│ │ (All-Reduce Sum)
└──► GPU 1: [W2_col] ──► GeLU ──► [W2_row] ──┴──► Output (Replicated)

A. Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP / FFN) Block

A standard Transformer MLP consists of two projections: Z=σ(XWgate)⊙(XWup)Z = \sigma(X W_{gate}) \odot (X W_{up})Z=σ(XWgate​)⊙(XWup​) followed by an output projection WdownW_{down}Wdown​.

  1. First Layer (Column-Parallel):
    • W1∈Rh×4hW_1 \in \mathbb{R}^{h \times 4h}W1​∈Rh×4h is sliced column-wise into [W1,1,…,W1,N][W_{1,1}, \dots, W_{1,N}][W1,1​,…,W1,N​], each of size h×4hNh \times \frac{4h}{N}h×N4h​.
      • Each rank computes Hi=σ(XW1,i)H_i = \sigma(X W_{1,i})Hi​=σ(XW1,i​).
      • Communication: 0 bytes.
  2. Second Layer (Row-Parallel):
    • W2∈R4h×hW_2 \in \mathbb{R}^{4h \times h}W2​∈R4h×h is sliced row-wise into [W2,1;… ;W2,N][W_{2,1}; \dots; W_{2,N}][W2,1​;…;W2,N​], each of size 4hN×h\frac{4h}{N} \times hN4h​×h.
      • Each rank multiplies its local intermediate activation HiH_iHi​ with W2,iW_{2,i}W2,i​: Y~i=HiW2,i \widetilde{Y}_i = H_i W_{2,i} Yi​=Hi​W2,i​
      • An All-Reduce sum collective is executed across the NNN ranks: Y=∑i=1NY~i Y = \sum_{i=1}^N \widetilde{Y}_i Y=i=1∑N​Yi​
      • Communication: Exactly 1 All-Reduce per MLP block.

B. Multi-Head Attention (MHA) Block

Attention naturally parallelizes across attention heads (hhh heads, each with head dimension dkd_kdk​):

  1. Q,K,VQ, K, VQ,K,V Projections (Column-Parallel):
    • The projection weights WQ,WK,WV∈Rh×hW_Q, W_K, W_V \in \mathbb{R}^{h \times h}WQ​,WK​,WV​∈Rh×h are sliced along columns such that each GPU receives hheadsN\frac{h_{\text{heads}}}{N}Nhheads​​ complete heads.
      • No communication is required to split attention heads; each rank gets its local Qi,Ki,ViQ_i, K_i, V_iQi​,Ki​,Vi​.
  2. Local Attention Computation:
    • Each rank performs scaled dot-product attention independently on its local head partition: Attentioni=Softmax(QiKiTdk)Vi \text{Attention}_i = \text{Softmax}\left(\frac{Q_i K_i^T}{\sqrt{d_k}}\right) V_i Attentioni​=Softmax(dk​​Qi​KiT​​)Vi​
      • Communication: 0 bytes.
  3. Output Projection (Row-Parallel):
    • The output projection matrix WO∈Rh×hW_O \in \mathbb{R}^{h \times h}WO​∈Rh×h is sliced row-wise: [WO,1;… ;WO,N][W_{O,1}; \dots; W_{O,N}][WO,1​;…;WO,N​].
      • Each rank computes O~i=Attentioni⋅WO,i\widetilde{O}_i = \text{Attention}_i \cdot W_{O,i}Oi​=Attentioni​⋅WO,i​.
      • An All-Reduce is executed to produce the unified context tensor: O=∑i=1NO~i O = \sum_{i=1}^N \widetilde{O}_i O=i=1∑N​Oi​
      • Communication: Exactly 1 All-Reduce per Attention block.

3. Forward vs. Backward Conjugate Collectives

Under reverse-mode automatic differentiation, the backward pass of a linear transformation swaps the transpose of the forward communication primitive:

Layer Type Forward Communication Backward Communication (Gradient ∇X\nabla X∇X) Backward Parameter Gradient (∇W\nabla W∇W)
Column Parallel None (Identity / Broadcast input) All-Reduce (∇X=∑i∇YiWi⊤\nabla X=\sum_i\nabla Y_iW_i^\top∇X=∑i​∇Yi​Wi⊤​) Local: X⊤∇YiX^\top\nabla Y_iX⊤∇Yi​
Row Parallel All-Reduce (Y=∑iXiWiY=\sum_i X_iW_iY=∑i​Xi​Wi​) None (Identity / Sliced ∇Y\nabla Y∇Y) Local: Xi⊤∇YX_i^\top\nabla YXi⊤​∇Y

Each Transformer layer requires:

  • Forward Pass: 2 All-Reduces (1 for Attention output, 1 for MLP output).
  • Backward Pass: 2 All-Reduces (1 across the input of Row-Parallel Attention, 1 across the input of Row-Parallel MLP).

4. Communication Overhead and Topology Constraints

A standard Ring All-Reduce transfers 2⋅N−1N⋅S2 \cdot \frac{N-1}{N} \cdot S2⋅NN−1​⋅S bytes for a tensor of size SSS.

For a Transformer layer with sequence length LLL, batch size BBB, and hidden dimension hhh:

  • The tensor transmitted in each All-Reduce is activation Y∈RB×L×hY \in \mathbb{R}^{B \times L \times h}Y∈RB×L×h.
  • In 16-bit precision (FP16/BF16), total bytes per All-Reduce: Bytes=2×B×L×h×2=4BLh \text{Bytes} = 2 \times B \times L \times h \times 2 = 4BLh Bytes=2×B×L×h×2=4BLh
  • Total forward communication per layer: VolumeFWD=2×2(N−1N)(2BLh)=8BLh(N−1N) bytes \text{Volume}_{\text{FWD}} = 2 \times 2 \left(\frac{N-1}{N}\right) (2BLh) = 8BLh \left(\frac{N-1}{N}\right) \text{ bytes} VolumeFWD​=2×2(NN−1​)(2BLh)=8BLh(NN−1​) bytes

Because this communication happens on every single Transformer layer in the critical path (blocking further GEMM computation), Tensor Parallelism has strict latency requirements:

  • Bandwidth bottleneck: Inter-node networking (e.g., 400 Gbps / 50 GB/s HDR/NDR InfiniBand) introduces high latency stalls relative to kernel execution times.
  • Hardware constraint: Tensor Parallelism is almost exclusively restricted to intra-node domains linked via high-speed interconnects (NVLink / NVSwitch at 900 GB/s to 1.8 TB/s per GPU). TP degree is typically set to N≤8N \le 8N≤8 (matching single-node GPU density).

5. Evolution: Sequence Parallelism (Megatron-SP)

In vanilla 1D TP, the operations outside the Attention and MLP blocks—specifically LayerNorm and Dropout—are replicated identically across all NNN ranks:

Vanilla TP:
Input ──► [LayerNorm (Replicated)] ──► [Col-GEMM] ──► ... ──► [Row-GEMM] ──► [All-Reduce] ──► [Dropout]

This causes two problems:

  1. Redundant compute for LayerNorm/Dropout.
  2. Activation memory for LayerNorm inputs/outputs cannot be sharded, dominating memory consumption at long contexts (L≥8kL \ge 8\text{k}L≥8k).

Sequence Parallelism (SP) solves this by observing that the All-Reduce operation in Row-Parallel linear layers is decomposed into:

All-Reduce=Reduce-Scatter+All-Gather \text{All-Reduce} = \text{Reduce-Scatter} + \text{All-Gather} All-Reduce=Reduce-Scatter+All-Gather

Instead of running an All-Reduce at the end of the row-parallel projection, Megatron-SP runs a Reduce-Scatter:

  1. The partial sums are reduced and simultaneously scattered along the sequence dimension (L/NL/NL/N).
  2. LayerNorm and Dropout execute on local slices of sequence length LN\frac{L}{N}NL​ with zero communication.
  3. Before the next Column-Parallel projection, an All-Gather reassembles the full sequence across all ranks.
Megatron-SP:
[Row-GEMM] ──► [Reduce-Scatter along S] ──► [LayerNorm on S/N] ──► [Dropout on S/N] ──► [All-Gather along S] ──► [Col-GEMM]

Communication volume remains identical to vanilla 1D TP (since Cost(Reduce-Scatter)+Cost(All-Gather)=Cost(All-Reduce)\text{Cost}(\text{Reduce-Scatter}) + \text{Cost}(\text{All-Gather}) = \text{Cost}(\text{All-Reduce})Cost(Reduce-Scatter)+Cost(All-Gather)=Cost(All-Reduce)), but activation memory from LayerNorm and Dropout drops by a factor of NNN.

item.title: Inference mem cost
item.description:
LLM inference memory and throughput fundamentally split across two operating regimes governed by the Roofline Model: the prefill phase (time-to-first-token, compute-bound) and the decode phase (token generation, memory-bandwidth-bound).

1. Total Inference Memory Breakdown

Total inference memory consists of static weights, the dynamic Key-Value (KV) cache, and transient runtime activation scratchpads:

Mtotal=Mweights+MKV+Mruntime_buffersM_{\text{total}} = M_{\text{weights}} + M_{\text{KV}} + M_{\text{runtime\_buffers}}Mtotal​=Mweights​+MKV​+Mruntime_buffers​

A. Model Weights (MweightsM_{\text{weights}}Mweights​)

Unlike training, inference requires no optimizer states and no gradients:

Mweights=N×PweightM_{\text{weights}} = N \times P_{\text{weight}}Mweights​=N×Pweight​

  • FP16 / BF16: 2 bytes / param2\text{ bytes / param}2 bytes / param →Mweights=2N\rightarrow M_{\text{weights}} = 2N→Mweights​=2N

  • FP8 / INT8: 1 byte / param1\text{ byte / param}1 byte / param →Mweights=1N\rightarrow M_{\text{weights}} = 1N→Mweights​=1N

  • INT4 (GPTQ / AWQ / GGUF Q4_K_M): ≈0.5 to 0.56 bytes / param\approx 0.5\text{ to } 0.56\text{ bytes / param}≈0.5 to 0.56 bytes / param →Mweights≈0.55N\rightarrow M_{\text{weights}} \approx 0.55N→Mweights​≈0.55N

B. KV Cache Memory (MKVM_{\text{KV}}MKV​)

For autoregressive generation, keys and values computed for previous tokens are stored in VRAM to avoid O(s2)O(s^2)O(s2) recomputation:

MKV=2⋅L⋅hKV⋅dhead⋅s⋅b⋅PKVM_{\text{KV}} = 2 \cdot L \cdot h_{\text{KV}} \cdot d_{\text{head}} \cdot s \cdot b \cdot P_{\text{KV}}MKV​=2⋅L⋅hKV​⋅dhead​⋅s⋅b⋅PKV​

  • 222: Stores both Key and Value tensors

  • LLL: Number of transformer layers

  • hKVh_{\text{KV}}hKV​: Number of KV heads (in Grouped-Query Attention / GQA, hKV≪hQh_{\text{KV}} \ll h_{\text{Q}}hKV​≪hQ​, typically 888 vs 323232)

  • dheadd_{\text{head}}dhead​: Head dimension (usually 128128128)

  • sss: Total sequence context length (prompt tokens + generated tokens)

  • bbb: Batch size (concurrent requests)

  • PKVP_{\text{KV}}PKV​: Bytes per element (222 for FP16, 111 for FP8, 0.50.50.5 for INT4)

Example (Llama 3.1 8B): L=32L=32L=32, hKV=8h_{\text{KV}}=8hKV​=8, dhead=128d_{\text{head}}=128dhead​=128, FP16 cache (2 bytes2\text{ bytes}2 bytes):

KV per token=2×32×8×128×2=131,072 bytes=128 KiB / token\text{KV per token} = 2 \times 32 \times 8 \times 128 \times 2 = 131,072\text{ bytes} = 128\text{ KiB / token}KV per token=2×32×8×128×2=131,072 bytes=128 KiB / token

For a batch of b=16b=16b=16 requests at context s=8,192s=8,192s=8,192:

MKV=128 KiB×8,192×16≈16.78 GBM_{\text{KV}} = 128\text{ KiB} \times 8,192 \times 16 \approx \mathbf{16.78\text{ GB}}MKV​=128 KiB×8,192×16≈16.78 GB

2. Autoregressive Decode Speed (Tokens / Sec)

In the token generation (decode) phase with batch size b=1b=1b=1, the GPU performs roughly 2N2N2N FLOPs per token. Because every model parameter must be fetched from HBM into SRAM once per token, the arithmetic intensity is:

Arithmetic Intensity=2N FLOPsMweights bytes≈2 FLOPs2 bytes=1.0 FLOP/byte\text{Arithmetic Intensity} = \frac{2N \text{ FLOPs}}{M_{\text{weights}} \text{ bytes}} \approx \frac{2 \text{ FLOPs}}{2 \text{ bytes}} = 1.0 \text{ FLOP/byte}Arithmetic Intensity=Mweights​ bytes2N FLOPs​≈2 bytes2 FLOPs​=1.0 FLOP/byte

Modern GPUs have an arithmetic intensity ceiling of 100–300 FLOP/byte100\text{–}300\text{ FLOP/byte}100–300 FLOP/byte, meaning compute units sit idle waiting for memory. Single-sequence generation speed is strictly memory-bandwidth bound.

Analytical Formula:

Throughput (Tokens/sec)=Memory Bandwidth (GB/s)×ηMBUBytes Read Per Token (GB)\text{Throughput (Tokens/sec)} = \frac{\text{Memory Bandwidth (GB/s)} \times \eta_{\text{MBU}}}{\text{Bytes Read Per Token (GB)}}Throughput (Tokens/sec)=Bytes Read Per Token (GB)Memory Bandwidth (GB/s)×ηMBU​​

  • ηMBU\eta_{\text{MBU}}ηMBU​ (Memory Bandwidth Utilization): Real-world kernel efficiency (typically 60% to 75%60\% \text{ to } 75\%60% to 75% in engines like vLLM, TensorRT-LLM, or llama.cpp).

  • Bytes read per token: Mweights+MKVbM_{\text{weights}} + \frac{M_{\text{KV}}}{b}Mweights​+bMKV​​ (at moderate contexts, MweightsM_{\text{weights}}Mweights​ dominates).

When concurrent batch size bbb increases (continuous batching), the static weights are read once and reused across all bbb sequences. Generation transitions from memory-bound to compute-bound when:

b∗≈Peak Tensor TFLOPsMemory Bandwidth (TB/s)×Weight Precision Bytesb^* \approx \frac{\text{Peak Tensor TFLOPs}}{\text{Memory Bandwidth (TB/s)} \times \text{Weight Precision Bytes}}b∗≈Memory Bandwidth (TB/s)×Weight Precision BytesPeak Tensor TFLOPs​

3. Hardware Comparison Matrix (Batch Size b=1b=1b=1, FP16 vs INT4)

Assuming sustained real-world ηMBU≈70%\eta_{\text{MBU}} \approx 70\%ηMBU​≈70%:

4. Batched Serving Throughput (Compute-Bound Scaling)

For cloud inference serving (e.g., serving 64 concurrent users simultaneously on an H100):

  • Single-user generation is latency-optimized (∼146 tok/s\sim 146\text{ tok/s}∼146 tok/s, GPU compute is mostly idle).

  • Batched generation (b=64b=64b=64) is throughput-optimized:

    Aggregate Tokens/Sec≈Active FP16 Tensor TFLOPS×MFU2⋅N⋅1012\text{Aggregate Tokens/Sec} \approx \frac{\text{Active FP16 Tensor TFLOPS} \times \text{MFU}}{2 \cdot N} \cdot 10^{12}Aggregate Tokens/Sec≈2⋅NActive FP16 Tensor TFLOPS×MFU​⋅1012

    (Each user receives 24,72564≈386 tokens/sec\frac{24,725}{64} \approx 386\text{ tokens/sec}6424,725​≈386 tokens/sec, achieving orders-of-magnitude better compute and hardware cost efficiency).

item.title: Training mem cost
item.description:
During LLM pretraining, memory overhead is divided into static state memory (model weights, gradients, optimizer states), dynamic activation memory, and runtime buffers/fragmentation.

1. Static Memory Breakdown (Per-Parameter)

For standard 16-bit mixed-precision training (BF16 / FP16 forward and backward passes) using the standard AdamW optimizer:

Component Precision Bytes / Parameter Formula

Optimizer Momentum (mmm) FP32 4 bytes4\text{ bytes}4 bytes 4N4N4N

2. Distributed Sharding Scaling (ZeRO / FSDP)

When distributing across KKK accelerator devices with Data Parallelism (DP=KDP = KDP=K):

Strategy Memory per Device (MstaticM_{\text{static}}Mstatic​) For 7B on 8 devices (N=7×109N=7\times10^9N=7×109, K=8K=8K=8)
No Sharding (Standard DDP) 2N+2N+12N=16N2N + 2N + 12N = \mathbf{16N}2N+2N+12N=16N ≈112 GB\approx 112\text{ GB}≈112 GB (OOM on 80GB GPU)
ZeRO-1 / FSDP Stage 1 (Shard Optimizer) 2N+2N+12NK=4N+12NK2N + 2N + \frac{12N}{K} = \mathbf{4N + \frac{12N}{K}}2N+2N+K12N​=4N+K12N​ ≈28+10.5=38.5 GB\approx 28 + 10.5 = \mathbf{38.5\text{ GB}}≈28+10.5=38.5 GB

    Mact≈b⋅s⋅L⋅h⋅(34+5⋅a⋅sh) bytesM_{\text{act}} \approx b \cdot s \cdot L \cdot h \cdot \left(34 + 5 \cdot \frac{a \cdot s}{h}\right) \text{ bytes}Mact​≈b⋅s⋅L⋅h⋅(34+5⋅ha⋅s​) bytes

Activation memory is the temporary GPU RAM used to store the intermediate tensors produced during the forward pass so that gradients can be computed via the chain rule during the backward pass.

1. Why Activations Are Stored

For any linear or matrix operation Y=X⋅WY = X \cdot WY=X⋅W:

  • The forward pass computes YYY.

  • The backward pass needs to compute the gradient with respect to weights:

    ∂L∂W=XT⋅∂L∂Y\frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial W} = X^T \cdot \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial Y}∂W∂L​=XT⋅∂Y∂L​

    To evaluate that product, the input tensor XXX must remain in memory until the backward pass reaches that layer.

2. The Analytical Formula (Without Checkpointing)

For a standard transformer layer, activations are stored at each operation: Attention (Q, K, V projections, attention matrix, softmax, output projection), Feed-Forward Network (FFN/MLP), LayerNorms/RMSNorms, and residual additions.

For a model with:

  • bbb = micro-batch size per GPU

  • sss = sequence length (context window)

  • hhh = hidden dimension

  • aaa = number of attention heads (where head dimension d=h/ad = h / ad=h/a)

  • Precision: 16-bit floating point (2 bytes per element2\text{ bytes per element}2 bytes per element)

The per-layer breakdown of stored elements:

Component Operation Stored Intermediate Tensors Bytes Stored (16-bit = 2×)
Self-Attention Inputs to Q,K,VQ, K, VQ,K,V projections XXX (b×s×hb \times s \times hb×s×h) 2bsh2 b s h2bsh
Attention score matrix (QKT/dQ K^T / \sqrt{d}QKT/d​) a×(b×s×s)a \times (b \times s \times s)a×(b×s×s) 2bs2a2 b s^2 a2bs2a
Softmax output a×(b×s×s)a \times (b \times s \times s)a×(b×s×s) 2bs2a2 b s^2 a2bs2a
Softmax dropout mask (if used) a×(b×s×s)a \times (b \times s \times s)a×(b×s×s) 1bs2a1 b s^2 a1bs2a (or 000 with FlashAttention)
Attention ×V\times V×V matrix product b×s×hb \times s \times hb×s×h 2bsh2 b s h2bsh
Projection out (WoW_oWo​) b×s×hb \times s \times hb×s×h 2bsh2 b s h2bsh
MLP / FFN Up-projection (standard 4h, or gated SwiGLU) 2 to 3×(b×s×h)2 \text{ to } 3 \times (b \times s \times h)2 to 3×(b×s×h) 16bsh16 b s h16bsh to 20bsh20 b s h20bsh
Norms & Residuals Pre-norm and post-norm inputs 2×(b×s×h)2 \times (b \times s \times h)2×(b×s×h) 4bsh4 b s h4bsh

Summing across all operations in one layer gives:

Mlayer≈b⋅s⋅h⋅(34+5⋅a⋅sh) bytesM_{\text{layer}} \approx b \cdot s \cdot h \cdot \left(34 + 5 \cdot \frac{a \cdot s}{h}\right) \text{ bytes}Mlayer​≈b⋅s⋅h⋅(34+5⋅ha⋅s​) bytes

Multiplying by the total number of layers LLL:

Mact≈b⋅s⋅L⋅h⋅(34+5⋅a⋅sh) bytesM_{\text{act}} \approx b \cdot s \cdot L \cdot h \cdot \left(34 + 5 \cdot \frac{a \cdot s}{h}\right) \text{ bytes}Mact​≈b⋅s⋅L⋅h⋅(34+5⋅ha⋅s​) bytes

Notice two distinct terms inside the parentheses:

  1. 343434 (Linear scaling with sss): Hidden state projections, norms, and FFN expansions (O(s)O(s)O(s)).

  2. 5⋅ash5 \cdot \frac{as}{h}5⋅has​ (Quadratic scaling with sss): Storing the raw s×ss \times ss×s attention matrices and softmax maps (O(s2)O(s^2)O(s2)).

3. How Checkpointing and FlashAttention Change This

Because storing every intermediate tensor causes memory to grow linearly with layer depth LLL and quadratically with context length s2s^2s2, modern training uses two primary optimizations:

A. Full Activation Checkpointing (Rematerialization)

  • Mechanism: Discards all intermediate activations inside each transformer block after the forward pass, retaining only the single input tensor entering each layer (b×s×hb \times s \times hb×s×h).

  • During Backward: Re-executes the forward pass for that block on-the-fly to regenerate the necessary activations.

  • Trade-off: Adds ~30–33% compute overhead (one extra forward pass), but reduces activation memory from O(L⋅s2)O(L \cdot s^2)O(L⋅s2) down to roughly:

    Mact≈2⋅b⋅s⋅L⋅h bytesM_{\text{act}} \approx 2 \cdot b \cdot s \cdot L \cdot h \text{ bytes}Mact​≈2⋅b⋅s⋅L⋅h bytes

B. FlashAttention (Tiling & Online Softmax)

  • Mechanism: Fuses the attention calculation into a single GPU SRAM kernel using online softmax. It never writes the large b×a×s×sb \times a \times s \times sb×a×s×s attention matrix to high-bandwidth memory (HBM).

  • Impact: Eliminates the quadratic O(s2)O(s^2)O(s2) memory term entirely, making attention memory scale strictly linear with sequence length sss.

4. Concrete Example: 7B Model (LLaMA Architecture)

  • Micro-batch size (bbb): 222

  • Sequence length (sss): 4,0964,0964,096

  • Layers (LLL): 323232

  • Hidden dimension (hhh): 4,0964,0964,096

  • Heads (aaa): 323232

Without Checkpointing (Vanilla PyTorch)

a⋅sh=32⋅40964096=32\frac{a \cdot s}{h} = \frac{32 \cdot 4096}{4096} = 32ha⋅s​=409632⋅4096​=32Bracket factor=34+(5×32)=194\text{Bracket factor} = 34 + (5 \times 32) = 194Bracket factor=34+(5×32)=194Mact≈2⋅4096⋅32⋅4096⋅194 bytes≈208.3 GBM_{\text{act}} \approx 2 \cdot 4096 \cdot 32 \cdot 4096 \cdot 194 \text{ bytes} \approx \mathbf{208.3\text{ GB}}Mact​≈2⋅4096⋅32⋅4096⋅194 bytes≈208.3 GB

(Exceeds the entire 80 GB VRAM of an A100/H100 from activations alone).

With FlashAttention + Selective Recomputation

Only the input to each layer and minimal non-recomputed buffers are retained:

Mact≈2⋅b⋅s⋅L⋅h bytes=2⋅2⋅4096⋅32⋅4096 bytes≈2.15 GBM_{\text{act}} \approx 2 \cdot b \cdot s \cdot L \cdot h \text{ bytes} = 2 \cdot 2 \cdot 4096 \cdot 32 \cdot 4096 \text{ bytes} \approx \mathbf{2.15\text{ GB}}Mact​≈2⋅b⋅s⋅L⋅h bytes=2⋅2⋅4096⋅32⋅4096 bytes≈2.15 GB

(Drops from 208 GB to ~2 GB per GPU, leaving ample headroom for weights and optimizer states).

item.title: ZeRO and FSDP
item.description:
Zero Redundancy Optimizer (ZeRO) and Fully Sharded Data Parallelism (FSDP) are memory optimization techniques that scale Data Parallelism by slicing a model’s memory footprint across multiple GPUs, enabling the training of models far larger than a single GPU’s VRAM limits.

Memory reduction across ZeRO Stages. Source: Medium

ZeRO Stage 1 (Optimizer State Partitioning) In standard data parallelism, every GPU holds a full copy of the optimizer states (like Adam’s momentum and variance), consuming massive memory. Stage 1 partitions these states across the cluster. Each GPU holds and updates only its assigned slice of the optimizer state.

ZeRO Stage 2 (Gradient Partitioning) Builds on Stage 1 by also partitioning the gradients. During the backward pass, a GPU computes gradients and retains only the specific slice it is responsible for updating, immediately discarding the rest to free memory.

ZeRO Stage 3 (Parameter Partitioning) The most aggressive form of ZeRO, dividing the actual model weights across all GPUs. No single GPU holds the full model. During forward and backward passes, a GPU dynamically fetches the required parameter slices from other GPUs using an All-Gather operation, computes the layer, and instantly discards the fetched weights.

ZeRO-Offload and ZeRO-Infinity Extensions of the ZeRO architecture that move optimizer states, gradients, or parameters out of GPU VRAM and onto CPU RAM or NVMe storage. This trades communication speed for massive capacity, allowing trillion-parameter model training on limited hardware.

Fully Sharded Data Parallelism (FSDP) FSDP is PyTorch’s native, highly optimized implementation of ZeRO Stage 3. It shards parameters, gradients, and optimizer states across data-parallel workers. FSDP wraps individual layers (like transformer blocks) and automatically manages the complex All-Gather (fetching weights before computation) and Reduce-Scatter (synchronizing gradients after computation) operations under the hood, making it the standard choice for modern PyTorch-based LLM training.

item.title: Online softmax
item.description:
The Standard 3-Pass Softmax Problem

Given an input vector x=[x1,x2,…,xN]x = [x_1, x_2, \dots, x_N]x=[x1​,x2​,…,xN​], standard numerically stable softmax prevents exponential overflow by subtracting the global maximum:

softmax(x)i=exi−m∑j=1Nexj−m,where m=max⁡jxj \text{softmax}(x)_i = \frac{e^{x_i - m}}{\sum_{j=1}^N e^{x_j - m}}, \quad \text{where } m = \max_{j} x_j softmax(x)i​=∑j=1N​exj​−mexi​−m​,where m=jmax​xj​

In conventional GPU implementations, this requires three separate memory passes:
